1: Your experiment has failed to produce the expected result three times in a row. Your first thought is:
I must have a step or parameter wrong. I'll review the whole procedure.
It's probably mostly my execution, though I'll check the reagents too.
It could be my work or an unstable batch. I need to investigate both.
These reagents or instruments have been unreliable lately, but I'll double-check my work too.
This batch of supplies or equipment is unreliable. Replacing it should probably fix things.
2: Your subproject has made little progress for over six months. You think the main reason is:
I don't understand the field well enough and chose the wrong methods.
Mostly my effort and approach, although resources really are tight.
My methods and the obscurity of the topic are equally responsible.
It's an obscure area with few resources, though I could probably push a little harder.
The topic is too obscure and the lab offers too little support. Anyone would struggle.
3: Your supervisor says your paper's logic is confusing. Your first private reaction is:
I really haven't clarified the main argument.
It's mostly my messy writing, with perhaps some miscommunication too.
Partly my problem, partly that this topic is inherently hard to explain.
This cutting-edge topic is complicated, though I could express it better.
My supervisor isn't familiar with this new field, so of course it seems confusing.
4: Your project proposal or competition entry was not selected. You think:
I haven't polished the proposal or work enough.
Mostly my work wasn't good enough, with a little bad luck too.
Ability and luck each account for about half of it.
The judges' preferences and luck mattered more, although I could improve.
The judges' judgment, connections and luck are what really matter.
5: Your calculation error cost the whole team a week of rework. When teammates ask, your first words are:
I calculated it wrong. It's my responsibility; I'll redo it and check the whole pipeline.
I mainly failed to catch it. The procedure is also tricky; I'll redo it.
I missed something, and the process has pitfalls too. Let's get it right first.
This analysis is easy to get wrong, and I didn't give it another check this time.
Anyone could make mistakes in this procedure. It isn't all on me.
6: You have repeatedly tried to read a difficult English-language paper without understanding it. You think:
My vocabulary and background knowledge aren't strong enough.
Mostly I lack the foundations, although the author's writing is convoluted too.
Half is my incomplete understanding; half is the paper's difficulty.
This paper really is badly written, though I should study more background too.
The author's logic is confused. Anyone would struggle to read it.
7: Your supervisor rejects your idea at a group meeting. You:
Think my argument wasn't strong enough and go back to gather evidence.
Think I mostly failed to explain it, though my supervisor may be a little conservative.
Think my argument and my supervisor's preferences may both play a part.
Think my supervisor is conservative, but I can make the case stronger too.
Think my supervisor is simply too conservative to accept new things.
8: A panel asks an unexpected question during your defense and you cannot answer. You think:
Mostly I failed to cover it, though the question was obscure too.
Half is my not anticipating it; half is how obscure it was.
That was a rather tricky question, though I should have prepared more.
That panelist's question was too obscure. Nobody could have answered it.
9: A peer who enrolled with you already has a first-author paper, and you do not. You think:
I really lag behind in topic choice and effort.
Mostly I've been slower, although their topic is easier to publish on.
My effort and their luck and topic each play a part.
Their topic is popular, with good resources and luck; I could still work harder.
They just have a popular topic, better supervisor resources and good luck.
10: Your paper is rejected. Your first reaction is:
There are serious weaknesses in its novelty or amount of work.
Mostly the paper isn't strong enough, and the reviewer was strict too.
Problems with the paper and reviewer luck may both matter.
This reviewer was strict or misunderstood it, though I can strengthen it too.
The reviewer didn't understand it. I was simply unlucky to get a strict one.
11: During a group demonstration, a senior colleague points out that your usual procedure is not standard. You think:
I haven't practiced enough or learned the details. I'll practice more.
Mostly I'm unfamiliar with it, though the procedure is counterintuitive too.
My unfamiliarity and the awkward procedure both matter; let's separate them.
The steps are convoluted, although I also need more hands-on practice.
The standard itself is counterintuitive. Anyone would make mistakes at first.
12: Your cells or laboratory animals suddenly deteriorate. Your first thought is:
I must have made an error in handling or environmental control.
I probably didn't care for them well, though the medium or batch may also be a problem.
We need to investigate my handling and the materials separately.
This serum or animal batch was unreliable, but I'll check my handling too.
This batch of materials or animals was poor quality. It isn't really my fault.
13: Halfway through graduate school, family and classmates keep saying a degree is useless and you should have started work earlier. You think:
Whether it's worthwhile is my choice; what I make of it mostly depends on me.
Mostly it depends on my effort, although the difficult job market is real.
My effort and the job market each account for about half.
Degrees are worth less these days; I'll just try to make the best of mine.
Whether graduate school pays off mostly depends on the market and luck, not me.
14: Your internship or job application is rejected. You think:
My skills or résumé weren't a good enough match.
Mostly I wasn't prepared enough, although competition was fierce too.
My ability and the job market each account for about half.
It's a competitive position and luck wasn't on my side; I can still improve.
Hiring is about connections and luck, not much about my ability.
15: Your interim report, data or other work is returned with many problems to fix. You think:
I didn't understand the requirements or pay enough attention to detail.
Mostly I misunderstood, although the requirements kept changing too.
My omissions and the vague requirements both share responsibility.
Anyone would struggle with changing requirements, though I can improve some things.
The requirements change daily and they don't know what they want. Don't blame me.
16: Reviewers request major changes to your research proposal. You think:
My preliminary research and design weren't solid enough.
Mostly I was underprepared, and the reviewers were demanding too.
My design and the reviewers' preferences both play a part.
These reviewers are strict, though my design can still be refined.
The panel is too picky and has set the bar too high.
17: After much experimental work, your statistical result is not significant. Your first reaction is:
My sample size or design is flawed.
Mostly it's my design, though the effect itself might also be weak.
Design problems and a weak effect need to be considered separately.
The effect is inherently small, although I could optimize the design.
Effects in this field are weak. Nonsignificance is normal and isn't my fault.
18: Classmates move into other careers or secure public-sector jobs while you stay in research. How do you view your path?
It's a choice I've thought through; whether it works depends on me.
Mostly on my own effort, with some influence from my institution and opportunities.
Personal effort and institutional resources each account for about half.
Success in academia depends a lot on supervisors and opportunities; I'll do my best.
An academic career mostly depends on resources and luck, not entirely on me.
19: Your survey or questionnaire responses are poor quality. You think:
My questionnaire design or recruitment method was flawed.
Mostly my design, although careless respondents contributed too.
My design and respondents' attitudes both matter.
Respondents were too careless, although I could phrase things better.
People just answer surveys randomly these days. The design has nothing to do with it.
20: You receive a warning at your midterm progress review. You think:
My output and effort really haven't been enough this term.
Mostly I haven't produced enough, although the topic is difficult too.
My effort and the topic's difficulty each account for about half.
This topic is slow to produce results, although I need to push harder too.
The one-size-fits-all standards ignore differences between topics. It isn't my fault.
21: A team project is due next week, but a teammate has not finished a core module. You:
Take over and finish their part too, to save the team.
Help them catch up while reminding them it's their responsibility.
Finish my part and help if needed, but their responsibility stays theirs.
Remind them to hurry; failure to finish is their problem.
It isn't my part. I'll just submit my own work.
22: A shared lab instrument breaks, and you did not break it. You:
Contact repair services and follow the issue through until it's fixed.
Report it for repair and mention it in the group chat.
Tell the group; whoever has time can follow up, not necessarily me.
Wait for its users or the equipment manager to deal with it.
I didn't break it. Act as though I haven't noticed.
23: A teammate's presentation slides are poor and will hurt the team. You:
Can't help stepping in and rebuilding them myself.
Give detailed suggestions and help revise a few key slides.
Point out the problems and let them fix the slides.
Do my own section; their presentation is their business.
We each present our own part. Their embarrassment isn't my concern.
24: Nobody is organizing the group's academic seminar. You:
Quietly handle the venue, invitations and refreshments myself.
Get it started and bring in two people to help.
Am willing to help, but everyone needs to share the work.
Wait for the supervisor to assign someone or for somebody else to act.
If nobody organizes it, we don't hold it. Nothing to do with me.
25: Nobody wants a shared chore, such as organizing the reference library. You:
Volunteer; somebody has to do it.
Make a start and ask everyone to share the work.
Am willing to do part, but would like a rota.
Wait for the supervisor to assign it; I'll act if it's assigned to me.
Leave it for now and wait for somebody else.
26: Your supervisor suddenly asks you to organize an intergroup meeting outside your duties. You:
Accept and use my own time to make it a success.
Accept, but explain that I have other work on my plate.
Check my schedule; do it if possible and explain any conflict honestly.
Give a vague yes and pass it to somebody else if possible.
Find a reason to politely decline; it isn't my responsibility.
27: Roles in a collaboration are unclear. Someone pushes their work onto you while you are already overloaded. You:
Take it and finish it without protest, fearing delays for everyone.
Handle it this time but make clear it was their responsibility.
Want to help but lack time; offer a manageable part and ask them to handle the rest.
Say yes, but drag my feet in practice.
Say it isn't my responsibility; everyone should do their own work.
28: Your code runs, but you notice a minor bug that would take half a day to fix. You:
Fix it immediately so it doesn't become a hidden problem.
Note it and fix it when I have time.
Assess its impact; fix it if important, otherwise put it on the backlog.
Leave it until it actually causes trouble.
Ignore it if it doesn't affect delivery.
29: Your supervisor asks you to teach a new junior colleague an experiment. You:
Teach every step and even help produce their preliminary data.
Teach carefully and watch them perform the key steps.
Explain the method, provide documentation and let them try, with questions welcome.
Give them some material to figure out, with brief answers if asked.
Let them figure it out; I'm busy with my own work.
30: A presentation error mainly came from a teammate's section. Your supervisor asks about it. You:
Cover for them and take some of the responsibility myself.
Explain which step failed and acknowledge that I didn't check it.
Explain each person's responsibility objectively, without exaggeration or blame shifting.
Mostly point to that step and say little about my own role.
Mostly point to that step and leave my failure to check unmentioned for now.
31: Junior colleagues keep interrupting your experiments with questions. You:
Patiently stop my own work and help every time.
Help when possible, but ask them to look things up first.
Set a regular question time and ask them to try independently otherwise.
Give a quick hint and ask them not to keep coming to me.
Am overloaded myself; let them work it out.
32: Your supervisor often asks you to collect parcels, order meals and run personal errands, just as your experiment becomes urgent. You:
Accept them all; even small requests deserve my best effort.
Usually help, and gently mention it when I truly cannot manage.
Help if it's on my way, but explain when it would clearly take research time.
Delay when possible and hope they ask somebody else.
These aren't my duties; find reasons to decline most of them.
33: Nobody is dealing with the group's reimbursements and paperwork. You:
Volunteer to handle everyone's claims together.
Do my own first and help organize the process along the way.
Do mine and propose a rota for shared tasks.
Handle only mine and leave everyone else's alone.
Leave the paperwork until somebody can't stand it and deals with it.
34: A peer upset by a research setback wants a long late-night talk, but you have an important experiment or presentation tomorrow morning. You:
Drop everything and stay with them until they feel better.
Listen and comfort them for a while, then suggest we both rest.
Offer immediate support, then suggest more professional help.
Give a few comforting words and suggest sleep and talking in daylight.
Can't really help and have too much to do; let them settle down themselves.
35: A classmate keeps trying to swap their undesirable shifts or rotations with you. You:
Almost always agree; happy to make life easier for others.
Swap when possible, but remember that they owe me a favor.
Judge each request; agree if reasonable and politely decline otherwise.
Usually find a reason to decline.
Never swap; everyone should work their own shifts.
36: Shared reagents or supplies are running out and nobody restocks them. You:
Quietly order more, regardless of who used them.
Restock and remind the group to log what they use.
Suggest a restocking rule and do it when it's my turn.
Let the supplies run out and wait for the person responsible.
I didn't use them all; restocking isn't my job.
37: A classmate wants extensive analysis for their paper. You are not an author and have your own work. You:
Agree to do it all as a favor.
Help, but make clear this workload deserves a contribution credit or authorship.
Help with small tasks; discuss authorship or roles before taking on a large workload.
Say I'm busy and avoid taking it on if possible.
Politely decline; it isn't my work.
38: An overloaded teammate wants to hand you administrative tasks that are their responsibility, such as sample collection or registration. You:
Take them all; doing a bit more is fine.
Help with some, while reminding them these are their duties.
Help in an emergency, but normally we each handle our own work.
Help occasionally, but decline if it happens too often.
Everyone owns their tasks; I won't carry theirs.
39: The shared group database has been neglected for years. You:
Take over long-term maintenance as the unpaid administrator.
Help clean it up once and write some usage guidelines.
Suggest dividing maintenance into modules and take one.
It's fine if it works; deal with it when it breaks.
If nobody else maintains it, neither will I, as long as it doesn't affect me.
40: During defense season, peers all ask you to revise their manuscripts or figures. You:
Help everyone, even if I have to stay up late.
Help as much as I can, prioritizing within my capacity.
Help a few close peers and give others guidance to revise things themselves.
Am short on time; give each a quick look and return it.
Have my own defense; no time to help.
41: Work is due the day after tomorrow. Tonight you develop a 39°C fever and can barely work. You:
Tell my supervisor tonight, explain the likely delay and propose a new submission time.
Send a message tonight saying I'm ill and may be late.
See if I can manage, and tell my supervisor first thing tomorrow if not.
Stay silent and try to push through until the due date.
Say nothing until my supervisor chases me, then mention I'm ill.
42: Halfway through an experiment, you discover you bought the wrong reagent, threatening the schedule. You:
Immediately tell my supervisor and propose replacement or alternatives.
Quickly explain it to my supervisor and ask what to do.
Look for an alternative first, then ask if unsure.
Make do with something else and don't report it yet.
Keep quiet and explain only when a real problem appears.
43: Two competitions or assignments turn out to overlap. You:
Immediately contact both sides to adjust timing or arrange a substitute.
Tell those involved soon and see what can be adjusted.
Try to arrange things myself first, then seek help if I can't.
Put it off and work something out closer to the date.
Say nothing until the conflict erupts.
44: Your supervisor asks for progress when you have only revised half the paper. You:
Specify exactly what's unfinished, what's blocking it and when it will be done.
Honestly say half remains and I'm working on it.
Give a rough update and catch up on the less clear parts myself.
Say 'nearly done' and buy another day if possible.
Avoid details and explain when I finally submit.
45: You need your supervisor's signature next week, but they will be away. You:
Get it signed a week early and explain its purpose.
Find time over the next few days to get the signature.
Ask when I remember and find another solution if I miss them.
Only remember to ask when I almost need it.
Wait until the deadline day and frantically contact them.
46: Your defense slides are ready, but your delivery feels hesitant. You:
Arrange rehearsals two weeks early and refine repeatedly.
Practice several times a few days beforehand.
Run through it when I can, then focus on practice nearer the date.
Start looking at it the night before.
Improvise at the venue and see how far I get.
47: Someone else's upstream task is stuck and will delay your work. You:
Proactively ask for progress, flag the risk and prepare a backup plan.
Ask what's happening and whether they need help.
Watch for a while and ask if nothing changes.
Say nothing until they fail to deliver.
Wait until I'm affected, then demand an explanation.
48: There is an uncertain value in the data you are about to present. You:
Clearly label it 'pending verification' and explain why.
Proactively mention that it still needs checking.
Keep it in mind and explain honestly if asked.
Gloss over it and hope nobody follows up.
Present it as certain and bet nobody notices.
49: You plan to go home for a week. You:
Arrange a handover in advance, with documentation and contact details.
Tell my supervisor several days early and organize my work.
Tell my supervisor before leaving and briefly explain the situation.
Mention it only the day before and give a casual handover.
Leave without much handover and deal with things later.
50: You suspect your experimental direction will fail and must present it next week. You:
Tell my supervisor about the risks and alternatives before the meeting.
Give my supervisor an early heads-up that progress is poor.
Report honestly at the meeting and explain details if asked.
Delay if possible and be vague at the meeting.
Wait until questioned in public and say 'the data are still running'.
51: You are changing rotations or research direction with unfinished work and materials left behind. You:
Prepare a handover checklist early and explain each item to the next person.
Explain the key points and pitfalls before leaving.
Give an overview and let them use my notes for details.
Give a few rushed words and leave.
I'm leaving anyway; let them figure out any problems.
52: A long-running experiment or task needs continuous care, but you must leave for several days. You:
Arrange reliable cover in advance with written care procedures.
Ask a colleague to watch it and explain the key steps.
Find someone just before leaving and hope nothing happens.
Take my chances and leave with little explanation.
Leave it alone and see how things are when I return.
53: You notice an omission in something you submitted that could affect later results. You:
Immediately report it through the proper process, correct it and keep a record.
Quickly tell the person responsible and add the missing part.
Quietly fix it myself first and ask about anything uncertain.
Fix it without saying anything; if nothing happens, leave it there.
Act as though I haven't noticed and wait until it's found.
54: Your project is about to exceed its budget. You:
Report early to my supervisor with expenses and a contingency plan.
Tell my supervisor soon that funds are tight.
Try to economize and report only if there still isn't enough.
Say nothing until the budget is actually exceeded.
Keep spending and let my supervisor deal with any problem.
55: Your delay will affect a collaborator's deadline. You:
Notify them immediately with the reason and a new delivery time.
Tell them soon that I may be a few days late.
Try to catch up first and tell them if I can't.
Wait until delivery is near before mentioning it.
Don't volunteer it; wait until they chase me.
56: Your equipment booking clashes with someone else's and will cause delays. You:
Coordinate early and proactively discuss different times.
Contact them as soon as possible to adjust it.
See who needs it most when the time comes.
Ignore it for now and deal with it then.
Wait until we meet at the instrument and argue it out.
57: Before submitting a paper, author or affiliation details need changing and coauthors need to know. You:
Immediately confirm with each person, then correct everything before submitting.
Quickly ask the group to check the changes.
Make the changes myself first, then ask everyone to check.
Submit first and slowly fix it later.
Don't bother asking everyone; submit using the old details.
58: The group meeting is approaching, but your analysis has not finished running. You:
Explain progress beforehand and present what is ready plus the remaining plan.
Honestly say at the meeting that it's still running and give a completion time.
Present what I can and say little about the unfinished part.
Avoid that section if possible and explain only if asked.
Vaguely say 'soon' and hope nobody presses me.
59: You discover a batch of follow-up data you manage is missing, which could affect results. You:
Proactively tell my supervisor or team and propose a recovery plan.
Tell the team about the gap soon.
Try to recover it myself and speak up if I can't.
Hide it for now and hope the impact is small.
Don't mention it; wait until the gap is found during analysis.
60: An external project's client suddenly changes the requirements, affecting your schedule. You:
Immediately update my supervisor and team and revise the plan.
Quickly tell the group that requirements have changed.
First assess whether I can absorb it, then decide whether to report it.
Take on the changes and speak up only when I can't cope.
Work quietly to the new requirements and explain when problems appear.
61: Your midterm defense is tomorrow. Tonight the main presenter quits; you are the unprepared backup. You:
Step up and prepare everything I can overnight.
Accept while finding a partner to share the load.
Assess whether I can manage; if not, honestly discuss alternatives with my supervisor.
Tell my supervisor I'm really unsure and ask them to find another solution.
Say I can't cover it and ask my supervisor to find someone else.
62: During your defense, a panelist asks you to run code you have not prepared. You:
Stay composed and write it on the spot or clearly explain the approach.
Give it a try while talking through it and improvising a recovery.
Admit I haven't prepared this part and explain the logic I do know.
Freeze, say something vague and quickly move on.
Cannot speak and wait for a teammate to rescue me.
63: The night before a major presentation, your core data do not match at all. You:
Find the cause, even if it takes all night.
Investigate while preparing an honest explanation of the situation.
Judge whether it can be rescued; if not, report honestly and request more time.
Feel uncertain and consider using old data to get through the presentation.
Act as though I haven't noticed and present as planned.
64: The night before submission, you find a reversed derivation. Recalculating could undermine the conclusion, takes much work and may miss the deadline. You:
Withdraw or recalculate as needed; I won't submit a conclusion I doubt myself.
Recalculate overnight; fix it if possible, otherwise proactively delay submission.
Assess the impact; withdraw if serious, or explicitly correct and annotate if minor.
Consider changing a few sentences to make it work and submit first.
Act as though I haven't noticed and submit unchanged, hoping nobody finds it.
65: Another group publishes your lab's main research direction first. You:
Immediately find a distinctive angle and salvage a paper.
Feel upset, but quickly regroup around another angle.
Take a day or two, then calmly assess what can still be done.
Feel discouraged for a long time and struggle to regain momentum.
Set the direction aside; I can't find the energy to return to it.
66: A critical experiment must run tomorrow. The lead is suddenly ill; you have never done the procedure, but the manual is available. You:
Study the manual until I understand the process and do it myself once confident.
Quickly review the manual, then ask someone experienced to guide me remotely.
Assess whether I can learn it in time; proceed if I can, otherwise escalate and explain.
Find reasons to avoid it and hope somebody rescues the situation.
Say I don't know how and ask my supervisor to find somebody else.
67: Your doctoral thesis review requires two additional experiments and may delay your defense. You:
Immediately plan parallel work and complete as much as possible.
Manage my emotions and work through a recovery plan step by step.
Assess feasibility and request a reasonable extension if necessary.
Put off the experiments and gain another day whenever possible.
Give up trying for now; if it's delayed, it's delayed.
68: Your supervisor recommends you for a major presentation, but you feel unqualified and fear being exposed. You:
Accept and prepare thoroughly to deliver under pressure.
Feel nervous but go ahead, rehearsing extra to build confidence.
Check whether I have enough preparation time before deciding.
Find a reason to pass the opportunity to someone else.
Decline outright and avoid that exposure.
69: Near graduation, you realize there is no time for extra experiments. You:
Make the most of the existing data and restructure the paper.
Find another defensible angle to salvage the work.
Discuss with my supervisor whether recovery or a reasonable extension makes sense.
Avoid facing it and hope I can somehow get through.
Stop trying and tell my supervisor I'll just extend.
70: After several days of late nights, your body is struggling, but a demanding task is due tomorrow. You:
Grit my teeth and finish the task first.
Push through the essential part and leave less important parts aside.
Assess my health and ask those involved for adjustments or time if needed.
Feel too drained and postpone everything I can.
Cannot keep going and simply leave it unattended for now.
71: You accidentally delete data from a shared folder. You do not know if it can be recovered, and others need it. You:
Notify those affected immediately, work on recovery and take responsibility.
Try recovery myself first and promptly explain if it fails.
Try recovery while assessing the impact and deciding who needs to know.
Say nothing for now and hope nobody notices or needs the data.
Act as though nothing happened; if asked, say I don't know how it disappeared.
72: Research feels increasingly unmotivating, and you keep thinking about switching to public-sector exams or other work. You:
Finish my current project responsibly while seriously planning whether and how to switch.
Set myself a decision deadline while continuing research and weighing my options.
Calmly assess which path fits me and talk with someone or my supervisor if needed.
Delay deciding, with less and less motivation for research.
Stay in limbo for now and take things as they come.
73: On the day of an important presentation, the computer or drive holding your data is lost. You:
Immediately find backups and try every recovery option to get through the presentation.
Look for backups while preparing an honest explanation.
Assess what can be recovered and explain honestly if it can't.
Panic and just want to escape the presentation.
Take leave or miss it; I don't want to face it.
74: Your stipend is low, money is tight and research fills your schedule. You:
Keep pushing through research while finding time for permitted aid or part-time work.
Find ways to earn more and spend less to get through this period.
Assess the situation and discuss support with my supervisor or school if needed.
Feel increasingly discouraged and lose motivation for research too.
Put things off where possible and just get by.
75: Family or relationship difficulties seriously conflict with your research progress. You:
Push hard on both fronts and try not to delay either.
Steady myself, prioritize both sides and work through them gradually.
Assess what matters most, explain to my supervisor and request breathing room if needed.
Feel overwhelmed and put research completely aside.
Don't want to face anyone and withdraw.
76: Thesis checks and reviews are approaching, and you feel close to your limit. You:
Break the work down and push through one task at a time.
Set a pace and keep moving while adjusting.
Slow down a little, talk or seek help, then continue.
Avoid it more as pressure rises and keep putting off starting.
Pause for now and delay another day whenever possible.
77: After three weeks of intense work, your body is sending clear warning signs, but a full data report is due this week. You:
Adjust my routine and push through to ensure report quality; deal with my health after submission.
Submit an adequate report that meets quality requirements, explain my condition and request time to add details.
Identify what can be simplified and what cannot, then find a workable balance before starting.
Hand in a half-finished report and tell myself it's good enough.
Really can't keep going; find a reason to request an extension. Health comes first.
78: For a while, your supervisor has kept rejecting your work and you are increasingly doubting yourself. You:
Adjust my mindset and respond with tangible progress, seeking outside support if needed.
Try not to unravel, talk with someone I trust and keep moving.
Calmly assess the relationship and seek communication or help through proper channels.
Withdraw more and try to keep a low profile until this period passes.
Lose motivation, set it aside and take things as they come.
79: Your paper keeps being rejected despite several rounds of revision. You:
Revise thoroughly again and submit to another journal.
Take a breath, analyze the comments and keep submitting.
Assess its potential and decide whether to continue or set it aside.
Lose confidence and avoid returning to it for a long time.
Give up on this paper and stop submitting it.
80: A delayed graduation is almost certain, and the pressure is overwhelming. You:
Accept reality and immediately start a recovery plan.
Take time to process it, then plan progress during the extension.
Assess calmly and discuss the next steps clearly with my supervisor.
Get stuck in my feelings and avoid facing the arrangements.
Stop trying for now and take things as they come.
